Billionaire Chase Coleman's Tiger Global Management raised its stake in Cerebras Systems (NASDAQ:CBRS) by 48.3% during the third quarter, according to the fund's 13F filed on Nov. 16, 2026. Tiger's share count rose from 2,999,000 as of June 30 to 4,446,347 as of Sept. 30. At quarter end, the position was worth $789.9 million.

Andrew Angelov / Shutterstock.com

Retirement-focused investors who watch what big funds buy should look at the thesis behind this recently public AI inference chipmaker before copying the trade.

How Much Weight Tiger Gives Cerebras

Cerebras made up 3.92% of Tiger's $20.17 billion in reported long positions across 45 stocks. That made it the fund's eighth-largest holding. Tiger's largest position was NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), valued at $2,740.6 million, or 13.59% of the book. So the fund added a newer AI chip name and kept its biggest weighting in the established leader. In this portfolio, Cerebras is a satellite holding around an NVIDIA core.

Other funds bought too. Of 13 tracked filers, 9 added shares, and Altimeter Capital opened a new position worth $1.01 billion. Coatue Management cut its stake.

Tech stocks aren't lacking in growth stories for 2027. The problem is that smart money is increasingly selective about which companies it's willing to pay a premium for. AI is still the big story, but skepticism is growing about whether the money invested will deliver the promised returns.

You could see that shift very clearly in the Bank of America fund manager survey for November. Investors were clearly pulling back from tech at the fastest rate since June 2006 (their net overweight position in tech fell from 37% in October to just 12%). Even more telling is that 38% of the 169 managers surveyed (who in total manage $461 billion) believe that firms are over-investing in AI and over half (52%) expect at least one of the major AI players to reduce its capital expenditure over the next 6 months.

The concerns led to a wider sell-off. The Nasdaq 100 Index is down over 10% in the second half of 2026. Semiconductors were particularly hard hit as investors have re-priced AI companies and rethought the sustainability of data center spending. This wasn't necessarily a rejection of AI per se. It was more a case of investors questioning how much expected growth had already been priced in.

There's still a lot of money flowing into the sector. JPMorgan expects AI-related capex to be $1.4tn in 2027, almost double its 2026 estimate. A significant portion will go into data centers, servers, networking gear and advanced semiconductors. For a closer look at where this spending is going, see our breakdown of the eight companies Morgan Stanley expects to spend $1.6 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2027. JPMorgan does, however, expect spending growth to tail off significantly from 2028.

The wider tech sector isn't moving in the same direction. Chip and data center suppliers are clearly on the up because of AI spending. On the other hand, the software and cloud businesses have to prove that their customers are actually going to spend more. For investors, it's all about separating the wheat from the chaff. Some businesses have sustainable demand while others are just in the midst of a spending spike.

The search for value is also playing out across the broader market. In a recent article, we look at 10 dirt-cheap stocks positioned to soar in 2027, focusing on companies that trade at attractive valuations despite strong expected revenue growth.

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) shares rose 0.26% to $491.18 at 10:55 a.m. ET on Friday, November 27, in the shortened regular session, as investors weighed an internal Code Red push to fix Microsoft 365 reliability. Memos reviewed by Reuters show the company wants to resolve future global incidents within an hour, a goal Microsoft 365 Core president Jason Henderson acknowledged it does not yet meet.

The trigger was a nearly 24-hour outage on November 12 and 13 that knocked out Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot. Microsoft's preliminary review traced it to a July fix for networking gateway servers and lock contention in an internal Windows process, leaving more than 80% of servers unresponsive at the worst point. Outage reports peaked at about 130,000 across 74 countries, TweakTown reported, and Satya Nadella apologized.

The GuruFocus chart shows a perfect GF Score of 100/100, with elite profitability, a strong balance sheet and top-tier momentum. The GF Value of $606.32 implies a 19.0% discount, which GuruFocus rates modestly undervalued, so the market is not treating the outage as lasting damage. The commercial risk is real, though: Copilot is sold on top of Microsoft 365, and every hour of downtime weakens the case for charging enterprises more per seat. The next test is Microsoft's final post-incident report and whether commercial bookings hold up next quarter.

title: Did Billionaire Bill Ackman Lose Confidence in Microsoft? The Answer Might Surprise You

Did Billionaire Bill Ackman Lose Confidence in Microsoft? The Answer Might Surprise You
Prosper Junior Bakiny, The Motley Fool

MSFT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Institutional investment managers are required to disclose their holdings quarterly through Form 13F, provided they meet certain criteria, within 45 days of the end of every quarter. Wall Street pays close attention to disclosures from the most famous managers, including Bill Ackman, the founder and CEO of Pershing Square Capital. And during the third quarter, Ackman oversaw what appears, at first glance, to be a significant decrease in Pershing Square Capital's stake in Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT). The fund apparently sold about two million of the tech leader's shares. Is Bill Ackman really bearish on Microsoft's prospects?

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

There is more to the story

Because hedge funds aren't required to disclose all of their financial assets, Form 13Fs do not necessarily capture a fund's full exposure to a particular company. That's what happened here. Ackman himself said in a post on X (formerly Twitter) that although his fund sold roughly two million shares of Microsoft during the third quarter, it also purchased long-term options giving it the right to buy about two million Microsoft shares at approximately $310 apiece -- these aren't required to be disclosed in Form 13F. The billionaire also said that he remains bullish on Microsoft and believes the stock is undervalued.

Ackman is onto something

Microsoft has underperformed the broader equity market this year, but it has gained significant value since late June. And the company's latest financial update gave the stock a boost. In the first quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Sept. 30, Microsoft's revenue increased by 19% year over year to $92.3 billion. Its non-GAAP earnings per share jumped 18% year over year to $4.89. Microsoft Cloud revenue was $63.9 billion, up 30% year over year.

And Azure revenue came in at $33.2 billion, up 48% compared to the year-ago period. Microsoft is cashing in on the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, and it is showing up in cloud revenue. The company ended the period with a commercial remaining performance obligation of $677 billion, up 73% year over year. The tech giant should experience strong sales growth within its cloud division for the foreseeable future. That's what the strong and growing backlog suggests.

Franklin Templeton (NYSE:BEN) is urging investors to rethink their stock market exposure heading into 2027, warning that excessive concentration in artificial intelligence stocks, elevated real interest rates and slowing earnings growth could create a more challenging investment environment.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 9 Warning Signs with BEN.

Is BEN fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

BEN GF Value chart

However, the investment management giant isn't suggesting investors abandon technology stocks such as Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL). Instead, it favors spreading investments across a wider range of businesses that could benefit from the technology.

For Americans investing through their 401(k)s, the warning is particularly relevant.

Investors holding traditional S&P 500 index funds (SPY) may have considerably more exposure to megacap technology companies than they realize because of the benchmark's market-cap-weighted structure.

Franklin Templeton favors equal-weighted indexes, active stock selection and businesses that can use emerging technologies to improve operating efficiency.

The firm also warns that elevated inflation-adjusted interest rates could weigh on economic growth and stock valuations while making fixed-income investments more attractive.

High-quality government bonds could provide some protection if economic growth deteriorates or enthusiasm surrounding technology stocks fades.

Franklin Templeton also identifies opportunities across infrastructure, private credit, venture capital and private equity secondary markets.

Investors Takeaway

For retirement savers, Franklin Templeton's outlook offers a compelling reason to examine their portfolio allocations heading into 2027.

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP), for instance, offers exposure to the same underlying companies as the traditional S&P 500 but reduces dependence on its largest constituents.

However, reducing megacap exposure could also mean missing out on substantial gains if technology stocks regain momentum.

Investors should monitor the relative performance of equal-weighted indexes, corporate earnings revisions and inflation-adjusted Treasury yields.

The biggest takeaway from Franklin Templeton's outlook is that investors don't necessarily need to abandon the market's biggest growth story to protect themselves against its growing risks.
